newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan approves tight budget in bid to trim deficit.
newsitem.headline: Japan approves tight budget in bid to trim deficit.

text.p: Japan's cabinet on Friday approved a tighter state budget for the next fiscal year in an effort to put its debt-ridden state finances in order.

With the economy showing signs of improvement, the Ministry of Finance's budget plan focuses on reducing the nation's accumulating debt instead of putting emphasis on strengthening the economic recovery.

Snowballing public debt and dwindling tax revenues have made Japan's budget deficit worse than those of other major industrialised nations such as the United States, which is now actively trying to balance its budget.

The budget for the fiscal year starting next April stood at 77.39 trillion yen ($678 billion), up three percent from the original budget for the 1996/97 year, which in turn was 5.8 percent larger than the original budget for the 1995/96 year.
Japan will issue 16.71 trillion yen ($146 billion) worth of government bonds to help finance next year's budget.
The ministry allocated a record 21.03 trillion yen ($184 billion) worth of new government bonds in 1996/97, of which 12 trillion yen ($105 billion) were deficit-financing bonds.
The draft budget is likely to be finalised on December 25, before being sent to parliament for approval in January.

Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka has said the government is aiming to cut bond issues, especially of deficit-financing bonds, by more than four trillion yen ($35 billion), in order to achieve Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's goal of making a strong start on fiscal reform in 1997/98.
The cabinet on Friday also approved a draft supplementary budget totalling 2.67 trillion yen ($23.4 billion) for the current fiscal year ending next March 31.
Tax revenues are estimated at 57.8 trillion yen ($507 billion) in 1997/98, up a considerable 12.6 percent from 51.35 trillion yen ($450 billion) in this fiscal year.

The ministry said the big revenue increase would be a result of a rise in the consumption tax to five percent from three percent in April, an end to special income tax cuts from January and expected economic growth of 1.9 percent in fiscal 1997/98.
These will boost tax revenues by about 6.4 trillion yen ($56.1 billion), a MOF official said.
On the expenditure side, the draft budget allocated 16.8 trillion yen ($147 billion) for debt servicing, up 2.6 percent from the original 1996/97 budget.
A government advisory panel said recently that Japan should aim for a "primary balance" of keeping spending -- excluding debt servicing costs -- below revenues in the next two to three years.
It also urged the government to keep the fiscal deficit at below three percent of gross domestic product by 2005.
"We were able to achieve primary balance in 1997/98," the official said.
General spending, the core of the budget, will total 43.81 trillion yen ($384 billion), up 1.5 percent from the amount earmarked in the original 1996/97 budget.
Under the budget, public works spending will grow only slightly, whereas in the past the government has spent large sums to help generate recovery momentum in the economy.
Japan will raise defence spending by 2.1 percent to 4.95 trillion yen ($43.4 billion) in 1997/98.
Japan, the world's top aid donor, plans to increase funding for its official development assistance programme by 1.3 percent to 1.16 trillion yen ($10.1 billion). ($1=114 yen)
